content: 1. The threshold for HBV DNA concentrations that defines inactive disease or the level above which treatment should be initiated is a critical parameter in clinical management. HBV DNA levels are also essential for monitoring the response to antiviral therapy, as an increase in these levels may indicate the emergence of resistant viral variants. 2. WHO standards now provide a uniform expression for HBV DNA concentrations, with conversions such as 10,000 copies/mL equating to 2,000 IU/mL, 100,000 copies/mL to 20,000 IU/mL, and 1 million copies/mL to 200,000 IU/mL. It is recommended to use the same assay consistently in the same patient to evaluate the efficacy of antiviral therapy. 3. Access to HBV DNA testing remains limited in resource-constrained settings, posing challenges for effective disease management. 4. Comprehensive assessment of liver disease severity includes clinical evaluation for signs of cirrhosis and decompensation, along with laboratory measurements of serum bilirubin, albumin, ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and prothrombin time. A complete blood count, including platelet count, is also necessary. 5. Routine investigations for liver disease include ultrasonography and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) measurement for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) surveillance, as well as endoscopy to detect varices in individuals with cirrhosis. 6. Liver enzyme levels, such as ALT and AST, may fluctuate over time, and single measurements do not reliably indicate disease stage. Typically, ALT levels are higher than AST levels, but this ratio may reverse as the disease progresses to cirrhosis. 7. Tests of liver synthetic function and/or portal hypertension include serum albumin, bilirubin, platelet count, and prothrombin time. A progressive decline in serum albumin, an increase in bilirubin, and prolonged prothrombin time are characteristic of decompensated cirrhosis. 8. Liver biopsy remains a method to determine the degree of necroinflammation and fibrosis, aiding in treatment decisions. However, it has limitations, including sampling error, subjectivity in reporting, high costs, risks of bleeding and pneumothorax, patient discomfort, and the need for specialized training and infrastructure, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). 9. Non-invasive tests (NITs) are increasingly replacing liver biopsy for assessing liver disease stage in chronic hepatitis B (CHB). These include blood and serum markers for fibrosis, such as APRI and FIB-4, as well as commercial markers like FibroTest or transient elastography (FibroScan), which can help rule out advanced fibrosis. 10. Screening for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is recommended for high-risk groups, including household and sexual contacts of CHB patients, HIV-infected individuals, people who inject drugs (PWID), men who have sex with men, sex workers, indigenous populations, incarcerated individuals, and transgender persons. Blood and organ donors should also be screened to prevent HBV transmission. 11. In regions with intermediate or low HBV endemicity, catch-up vaccination and preventive strategies are targeted at adolescents, household and sexual contacts of HBsAg-positive individuals, and high-risk groups such as PWID and individuals with multiple sexual partners. 12. Antiviral therapy is crucial for individuals with CHB at high risk of disease progression to reduce morbidity. While nucleos(t)ide analogues (NAs) effectively inhibit HBV replication, they rarely result in a cure, necessitating long-term or lifelong therapy. NAs are preferred over interferon (IFN) due to fewer side effects and oral administration, but IFN offers advantages such as the absence of resistance and higher rates of HBeAg and HBsAg loss. 13. New treatment strategies, such as tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF), aim to enhance drug delivery to hepatocytes while minimizing toxicity. Research is ongoing to develop curative therapies targeting all replicative forms of HBV, including covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA). 14. Coinfection with HBV and other viruses like HIV, HCV, or HDV often results in more severe liver disease and higher rates of cirrhosis, HCC, and mortality. Management of coinfections requires tailored approaches, as these conditions can accelerate disease progression. 15. In children, CHB is generally asymptomatic and benign, often in the immune-tolerant phase. Treatment is typically reserved for those with severe necroinflammatory disease or cirrhosis. Approved therapies for children include tenofovir for those over 12 years and entecavir for those over 2 years. 16. Non-invasive assessment of liver disease stage, such as APRI or FibroScan, is recommended at baseline and during follow-up, particularly in resource-limited settings.
